summary.text: The Bonferroni inequalities are upper and lower bounds on the probability of a finite union of events.
They generalize Boole's inequality for a finite number of events, and are named after Carlo Emilio Bonferroni, with a reference dated 1936.
The Bonferroni Method of simultaneous inference uses the same idea: to make five estimates all good with 95% chance, each one is made good to 99%.

facts.label: What they bound
facts.value: The probability of finite unions of events

items.prompt: A lab estimates five quantities from one random sample and controls each separately. It wants all five to be good with 95% chance. How much chance of being wrong can it allow for each one?

options.label: 5% each, the same as the total
10% each, since errors may cancel
0.25% each, to be extra safe
1% each, an equal share of the 5%

items.explain: The allowed 5% chance of failure is split over the five estimates, giving 0.05/5 = 0.01 each.

items.prompt: Each of five estimates is built with a 99% confidence interval, yet the lab only promises 95% for all five together. Why is 99% used for each?

options.label: Because the total error budget has to be shared among the five
Because five estimates always lose 4% of confidence in total
Because 99% intervals are always wider than 95% ones
Because the sample must be five times larger

items.explain: To make the whole set good with 95% chance, each estimate is guaranteed good to 99%, so the 5% failure allowance is split five ways.

items.prompt: Boole's inequality for a finite number of events can be generalized. What does the generalization tell you about the chance that at least one of the events happens?

options.label: A single exact value for that chance
One fixed upper bound and no floor
A lower bound with no matching ceiling
Certain upper and lower bounds on that chance

items.explain: The generalization gives upper and lower bounds on the probability of finite unions of events, called the Bonferroni inequalities.

items.prompt: A statistician controls five estimates one at a time and wants a joint guarantee. What is the name of the approach of splitting the allowed error among them?

options.label: The Boole method of countable limits
The Bonferroni Method of simultaneous inference
The Kolmogorov method of unit measure
The Lebesgue method of measurable sets

items.explain: Making each estimate good enough that the total is good with the chosen chance is called the Bonferroni Method of simultaneous inference.

items.prompt: Someone hands you a family of bounds on the chance that one of several events occurs, and says they are all upper bounds. What do the Bonferroni inequalities say about this?

options.label: Some are upper bounds and others are lower bounds
All of them are upper bounds, as claimed
All of them are lower bounds, so the claim is reversed
They give exact values rather than bounds

items.explain: The Bonferroni inequalities are upper and lower bounds on the probability of finite unions of events.

paragraphs.heading: Bounds on a union
paragraphs.text: Boole's inequality, stated for a finite number of events, can be stretched into a family of upper and lower bounds. These bounds limit the probability of a finite union of events from above and from below. They carry the name of Carlo Emilio Bonferroni, and his work is cited as Bonferroni (1936).

paragraphs.heading: Where they come from
paragraphs.text: The Bonferroni inequalities are consequences of the inclusion–exclusion principle. Boole's inequality sits inside the family as the special case where K = 1. Boole's inequality itself comes in a finite version and a countable version. The countable one is reached from the finite one by letting the number of events n grow without end and using the continuity from below of probability measures.

paragraphs.heading: Not only for probability
paragraphs.text: Proving the inclusion–exclusion principle needs very little: only that P is finitely additive and never negative. Because of that, the Bonferroni inequalities keep working when P is swapped for any finite content, a notion from measure theory. In the same spirit, Boole's inequality is a case of the countable subadditivity of measures, so it holds for arbitrary measures and not just probability measures.

paragraphs.heading: A five-part estimate
paragraphs.text: Picture a task where you estimate five parameters from one random sample, and you can tune the accuracy of each one on its own. You want all five estimates to be good at once, with a 95% chance. The question is how strict to be with each single estimate. One answer is to set each of them to 0.05/5 = 0.01, which is 1%.

paragraphs.heading: The Bonferroni method
paragraphs.text: Put another way, each single estimate must be made good to 99%, for instance by building a 99% confidence interval for it. Doing that for all five guarantees that the whole set of estimates is good with a 95% chance. This recipe is known as the Bonferroni Method of simultaneous inference.
